species.real: Brunel lost the 'gauge war': a Royal Commission and the Gauge Act of 1846 favoured George Stephenson's narrower gauge, which is still standard on most of the world's railways.
species.name: Gaugelet

dex.text: Wears a stovepipe hat two sizes too tall and keeps a stub of pencil behind its ear. Measures everything twice, then builds it bigger anyway.
dex.fact: Isambard Kingdom Brunel built the Great Western Railway from London to Bristol on a broad gauge of 7 feet and a quarter of an inch; the last broad-gauge trains ran in 1892.

species.real: Brunel's Great Eastern, launched in 1858, was so huge that no ship beat her size for about forty years, and she went on to lay the first lasting transatlantic telegraph cable in 1866.
species.name: Broadgauge

dex.text: Thunders down the line with its chains clanking and its funnel hat steaming, and will not hear a word said for narrow gauge. Sparks fly when it brakes. It rarely brakes.
dex.fact: Brunel's SS Great Britain, launched in Bristol in 1843, was the first iron-hulled, propeller-driven ship to cross the Atlantic.
